entries.739c14d03061cefec3996f7c9ddd2496018cd130: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv105"/><title type="x-ms">Zechariah</title> <div sID="gen20753" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20754" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> prophet was colleague with the prophet Haggai, and a worker together with him in forwarding the building of the second temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1">Ezra v. 1</reference>); for two are better than one. Christ sent forth his disciples two and two. Zechariah began to prophesy some time after Haggai. But he continued longer, soared higher in visions and revelations, wrote more, and prophesied more particularly concerning Christ, than Haggai had done; so <hi type="italic">the last shall be first:</hi> the last in time sometimes proves first in dignity. He begins with a plain practical sermon, expressive of that which was the scope of his prophesying, in the <reference osisRef="Zech.1.1-Zech.1.5">first five verses</reference>; but afterwards, to the end of <reference osisRef="Zech.6.1-Zech.6.15">ch. vi.</reference>, he relates the visions he saw, and the instructions he received immediately from heaven by them. At <reference osisRef="Zech.7.1-Zech.7.14">ch. vii.</reference>, from an enquiry made by the Jews concerning fasting, he takes occasion to show them the duty of their present day, and to encourage them to hope for God's favour, to the end of <reference osisRef="Zech.8.1-Zech.8.23">ch. viii.</reference>, after which there are two sermons, which are both called <hi type="italic">burdens of the word of the Lord</hi> (one begins with <reference osisRef="Zech.9.1-Zech.9.17">ch. ix.</reference>, the other with <reference osisRef="Zech.12.1-Zech.12.14">ch. xii.</reference>), which probably were preached some time after; the scope of them is to reprove for sin, and threaten God's judgments against the impenitent, and to encourage those that feared God with assurances of the mercy God had in store for his church, and especially of the coming of the Messiah and the setting up of his kingdom in the world. <div eID="gen20754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20755" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20756" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, after the introduction (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">ver. 1</reference>), we have, I. An awakening call to a sinful people to repent of their sins and return to God, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.2-Zech.1.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. II. Great encouragement given to hope for mercy. 1. By the vision of the horses, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.7-Zech.1.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. 2. By the prayer of the angel for Jerusalem, and the answer to that prayer, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.12-Zech.1.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. 3. By the vision of the four carpenters that were employed to cut off the four horns with which Judah and Jerusalem were scattered, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.18-Zech.1.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv105"/> <div eID="gen20756" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20755" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Repentance Urged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20757" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath been sore displeased with your fathers. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore say thou unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">4</hi> Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Turn ye now from your evil ways, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> your evil doings: but they did not hear, nor hearken unto me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> Your fathers, where <hi type="italic">are</hi> they? and the prophets, do they live for ever? <hi type="super">6</hi> But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers? and they returned and said, Like as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts thought to do unto us, according to our ways, and according to our doings, so hath he dealt with us. <div eID="gen20757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20758" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The foundation of Zechariah's ministry; it is laid in a divine authority: <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord came to him.</hi> He received a divine commission to be God's mouth to the people and with it instructions what to say. He received of the Lord that which also he delivered unto them. <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord was to him;</hi> it came in the evidence and demonstration of the Spirit, as a real thing, and not a fancy. For the ascertaining of this, we have here, 1. The time when the word of the Lord came first to him, or when the word that next follows came to him: it was <hi type="italic">in the second year of Darius.</hi> Before the captivity the prophets dated their writings by the reigns of the kings of Judah and Israel; but now by the reigns of the kings of Persia, to whom they were subjects. Such a melancholy change had sin made of their circumstances. Zerubbabel took not so much state upon him as to have public acts dated by the years of his government, and in things of this nature the prophets, as is fit, complied with the usage of the time, and scrupled not to reckon by the years of the heathen kings, as <reference osisRef="Dan.7.1">Dan. vii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1">viii. 1</reference>. Zechariah preached his first sermon in the <hi type="italic">eighth month</hi> of this <hi type="italic">second year</hi> of Darius; Haggai preached his in the sixth month of the same year, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag. i. 1</reference>. The people being readily obedient to the word of the Lord in the mouth of Haggai, God blessed them with another prophet; for to him that has, and uses well what he has, more shall be given. 2. The name and family of the prophet to whom the word of the Lord came; He was <hi type="italic">Zechariah, the son of Barachiah, the son of Iddo,</hi> and he was <hi type="italic">the prophet,</hi> as Haggai is called <hi type="italic">the prophet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag. i. 1</reference>. For, though in former ages there was one Iddo a prophet (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.15">2 Chron. xii. 15</reference>), yet we have no reason to think that Zechariah was of his progeny, or should be denominated from him. The learned Mr. Pemble is decidedly of opinion that this Zechariah, the son of Barachiah, is the same that our Saviour says was <hi type="italic">slain between the temple and the altar,</hi> perhaps many years after the rebuilding of the temple (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Matt. xxiii. 35</reference>), and that our Saviour does not mean (as is commonly thought) Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, for why should Jehoiada be called Barachiah? And he thinks the manner of Christ's account persuades us to think so; for, reckoning up the innocent blood shed by the Jews, he begins at Abel, and ends even in the last of the holy prophets. Whereas, after Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, many prophets and righteous men were put to death by them. It is true there is no mention made in any history of their slaying this Zechariah, but Josephus might industriously conceal that shame of his nation. Perhaps what Zechariah spoke in his prophesying concerning Christ of his being sold, his being wounded in the house of his friends, and the shepherd being smitten, was verified in the prophet himself, and so he became a type of Christ. Probably, being assaulted by his persecutors, he took sanctuary in the court of the priests (and some think he was himself a priest), and so was slain between the porch and the altar. <div eID="gen20758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20759" type="x-p"/> II. The first-fruits of Zechariah's ministry. Before he came to visions and revelations, and delivered his prophetic discourses, he preached that which was plain and practical; for it is best to begin with that. Before he published the promises of mercy, he published calls to repentance, for thus <hi type="italic">the way of the Lord</hi> must be <hi type="italic">prepared.</hi> Law must be first preached, and then gospel. Now, <div eID="gen20759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20760" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophet here puts them in mind of the controversy God had had with their fathers (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord has been sorely displeased with your fathers,</hi> and has laid them under the tokens of his displeasure. You have heard with your ears, and your fathers have told you of it; you have seen with your eyes the woeful remains of it. God's quarrel with you has been of long standing, and therefore it is time for you to think of taking it up." Note, The judgments of God, which those that went before us were under, should be taken as warnings to us not to tread in their steps, and calls to repentance, that we may cut off the entail of the curse and get it turned into a blessing. <div eID="gen20760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20761" type="x-p"/> 2. He calls them, in God's name, to return to him, and make their peace with him, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.3">v. 3</reference>. God by him says that to this backsliding people which he had often said by his servants the prophets: "<hi type="italic">Turn you to me</hi> in a way of faith and repentance, duty and obedience, and <hi type="italic">I will turn to you</hi> in a way of favour and mercy, peace and reconciliation." Let the rebels return to their allegiance, and they shall be taken under the protection of the government and enjoy all the privileges of good subjects. Let them change their way, and God will change his. See <reference osisRef="Mal.3.7">Mal. iii. 7</reference>. But that which is most observable here is that God is called here the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts</hi> three times: "<hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord of hosts.</hi> It is he that speaks, and therefore you are bound to regard what he says." <hi type="italic">Turn you to me, saith the Lord of hosts</hi> (this intimates the authority and obligation of the command), <hi type="italic">and I will turn to you, saith the Lord of hosts</hi>—this intimates the validity and value of the promise; so that it is no vain repetition. Note, The consideration of God's almighty power and sovereign dominion should both engage and encourage sinners to repent and turn to him. It is very desirable to have the Lord of hosts our friend and very dreadful to have him our enemy. <div eID="gen20761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20762" type="x-p"/> 3. He warns them not to persist in their impenitence, as their fathers had done (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be you not as your fathers.</hi> Instead of being hardened in their evil courses by the example of their fathers' sins, let them rather be deterred from them by the example of their fathers' punishment. We are apt to be governed very much by precedent, and we are well or ill governed according to the use we make of the precedents before us. The same examples to some are a savour of life unto life, to others a savour of death unto death. Some argued, "Shall we be wiser than our fathers? They never minded the prophets, and why then should we mind them? They made laws against them, and why should we tolerate them?" But they are here taught how they should argue: "Our fathers slighted the prophets, and God was sorely displeased with them for it; therefore let us the more carefully regard what God says to us by his prophets." "Review what is past, and observe," <div eID="gen20762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20763" type="x-p"/> (1.) "What was the message that God sent by his servants the prophets to your fathers: <hi type="italic">The former prophets cried to your fathers.</hi> cried aloud, and did not spare, not spare themselves, not spare your fathers; they cried as men in earnest, as men that would be heard; they spoke not as from themselves, but in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts;</hi> and this was the substance of what they said, the burden of every song, the application of every sermon—<hi type="italic">Turn you now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings;</hi> the very same that we now preach to you. Be persuaded to leave your sins; resolve to have no more to do with them. A speedy reformation is the only way to prevent an approaching ruin: <hi type="italic">Turn you now</hi> from sin to God without delay." <div eID="gen20763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20764" type="x-p"/> (2.) "How little this message was regarded by your fathers: <hi type="italic">But they did not hear,</hi> they did not heed. They turned a deaf ear to these calls: <hi type="italic">They would not hearken unto me, saith the Lord.</hi> They would not be reclaimed, would not be ruled, by the word I sent them; say not then that you will do as your fathers did, for they did amiss;" see <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer. xliv. 17</reference>. Note, We must not follow the examples of our dear fathers unless they were God's dear children, nor any further than they were dutiful and obedient to him. <div eID="gen20764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20765" type="x-p"/> (3.) "What has become both of your fathers and of the prophets that preached to them? They are all dead and gone," <reference osisRef="Zech.1.5">v. 5</reference>. [1.] <hi type="italic">Your fathers, where are they?</hi> The whole generation of them is swept away, and their place knows them no more. Note, When we think of our ancestors, that have gone through the world and gone out of it before us, we should think, <hi type="italic">Where are they?</hi> Here they were, in the towns and countries where we live, passing and repassing in the same streets, dwelling in the same houses, trading in the same shops and exchanges, worshipping God in the same churches. But where are they? They are somewhere still; when they died there was not an end of them. They are in eternity, in the world of spirits, the unchangeable world, to which we are hastening apace. Where are they? Those of them that lived and died in sin are in torment, and we are warned by Moses and the prophets, Christ and his apostles, to look to it that we <hi type="italic">come not to that place of torment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.28-Luke.16.29">Luke xvi. 28, 29</reference>. Those of them that lived and died in Christ are in paradise; and, if we live and die as they did, we shall be with them shortly, with them eternally. [2.] <hi type="italic">The prophets</hi> also, <hi type="italic">did they live for ever?</hi> No, they are gone too. The treasure is put into earthen vessels, the water of life into earthen pitchers, often cracked, and brought home broken at last. Christ is a prophet that lives for ever, but all other prophets have a period put to their office. Note, Ministers are dying men, and live not for ever in this world. They are to look upon themselves as such, and to preach accordingly, as those that must be silenced shortly, and know not which sermon may be the last. People are to look upon them as such, and to hear accordingly, as those that yet a little while have the <hi type="italic">light with them,</hi> that they may walk and work <hi type="italic">while they have the light.</hi> Oh that this weighty consideration had its due weight given it, that we are dying ministers dealing with dying people about the concerns of immortal souls and an awful eternity, which both they and we are standing upon the brink of! It concerns us to think of the prophets that are gone, that were <hi type="italic">before us of old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.28.8">Jer. xxviii. 8</reference>. Those that were the glory of men withered and fell; but the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord endures for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24-1Pet.1.25">1 Pet. i. 24, 25</reference>. The prophets that are now, do <hi type="italic">we live for ever?</hi> (so some read it); no, Haggai and Zechariah will not be long with you, and prophecy itself shall shortly cease. In another world both we and our prophets shall live for ever; and to prepare for that world ought to be our great care and business in this. <div eID="gen20765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20766" type="x-p"/> (4.) "What were the effects of the word which God spoke to them by his prophets, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.6">v. 6</reference>. The preachers died, and the hearers died, but the word of God died not; that took effect, and not one iota or tittle of it fell to the ground." As the <hi type="italic">rain</hi> and <hi type="italic">snow</hi> from heaven, <hi type="italic">it shall not return void,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Isa. lv. 11</reference>. He appealed to themselves; they knew very well, [1.] That the judgments God had threatened were executed upon their fathers, and they were made to feel what they would not believe and fear: "<hi type="italic">My statutes which I commanded my servants the prophets,</hi> the precepts with the penalties annexed, which I charged them with the delivery of, <hi type="italic">did they not take hold of your fathers?</hi>" Though God's prophets could not fasten convictions upon them, the calamities threatened overtook them, and they could not escape them, nor get out of the reach of them. God's words took hold of them as the bailiff arrests the debtor, and takes him in execution for contempt. Note, The unbelief of man cannot make the threatenings of God's word of no effect, but, sooner or later, they will take place, if the prescribed course be not taken to prevent the execution of them. God's anger will certainly take hold of those that will not be taken hold of by his authority; for when he judges he will overcome. [2.] That they themselves could not but own the accomplishment of the word of God in the judgments of God that were upon them, and that therein he was righteous, and had done them no wrong: <hi type="italic">They returned, and said</hi> (they changed their mind, and when it was too late to prevent the ruin of their nation they acknowledged), <hi type="italic">Like as the Lord of hosts thought to do unto us according to our ways and doings,</hi> to reckon with us for them, <hi type="italic">so has he dealt with us,</hi> and we must acknowledge both his truth and his justice, must blame ourselves only, and have no blame to lay to him. <hi type="italic">Sero sapiunt Phryges—It is late before the Phrygians become wise.</hi> This after-wit, as it is a proof of the truth of God, so it is a proof of the folly of men, who will look no further than they can see. They would never be persuaded to say in time, "God will be as good as his word, for he is faithful; he will deal with us according to our deserts, for he is righteous." But now they see both plainly enough when the sentence is executed; now he that runs may read, and publish the exact agreement that appears between the present providences and the former predictions which then were slighted, between the present punishments and the former sins which then were persisted in. Now they cannot but say, <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.11-Dan.9.13">Dan. ix. 11-13</reference>.
entries.f2fb89d110508102d85720a9079283d9da4990ce: <div eID="gen20766" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Horse and Myrtles; Intercession for Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20767" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Upon the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the month Sebat, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying, <hi type="super">8</hi> I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the bottom; and behind him <hi type="italic">were there</hi> red horses, speckled, and white. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then said I, O my lord, what <hi type="italic">are</hi> these? And the angel that talked with me said unto me, I will shew thee what these <hi type="italic">be.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the man that stood among the myrtle trees answered and said, These <hi type="italic">are they</hi> whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they answered the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that stood among the myrtle trees, and said, We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered and said, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years? <hi type="super">13</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered the angel that talked with me <hi type="italic">with</hi> good words <hi type="italic">and</hi> comfortable words. <hi type="super">14</hi> So the angel that communed with me said unto me, Cry thou, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I am very sore displeased with the heathen <hi type="italic">that are</hi> at ease: for I was but a little displeased, and they helped forward the affliction. <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem. <hi type="super">17</hi> Cry yet, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; My cities through prosperity shall yet be spread abroad; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem. <div eID="gen20767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20768" type="x-p"/> We not come to visions and revelations of the Lord; for in that way God chose to speak by Zechariah, to awaken the people's attention, and to engage their humble reverence of the word and their humble enquiries into it, and to fix it the more in their minds and memories. Most of the following visions seem designed for the comfort of the Jews, now newly returned out of captivity, and their encouragement to go on with the building of the temple. The scope of this vision (which is as an introduction to the rest) is to assure the Jews of the care God took of them, and the eye of his providence that was upon them for good, now in their present state, when they seem to be deserted, and their case deplorable. The vision is dated (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.7">v. 7</reference>) <hi type="italic">the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month,</hi> three months after he preached that sermon (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">v. 1</reference>), in which he calls them to repentance from the consideration of God's judgments. Finding that that sermon had a good effect, and that they returned to God in a way of duty, the assurances he had given them are confirmed, that God would return to them in a way of mercy. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20769" type="x-p"/> I. What the prophet saw, and the explication of that. 1. He saw a grove of <hi type="italic">myrtle-trees,</hi> a dark shady grove, down <hi type="italic">in a bottom,</hi> hidden by the adjacent hills, so that you were not aware of it till you were just upon it. This represented the low, dark, solitary, melancholy condition of the Jewish church at this time. They were over-topped by all their neighbours, buried in obscurity; what friends they had were hidden, and there appeared no way of relief and succour for them. Note, The church has not been always visible, but sometimes hidden, as the <hi type="italic">woman in the wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">Rev. xii. 6</reference>. 2. He saw <hi type="italic">a man</hi> mounted upon <hi type="italic">a red horse,</hi> standing in the midst of this shady myrtle-grove. This man is no other than the <hi type="italic">man Christ Jesus,</hi> the same that appeared to Joshua with <hi type="italic">his sword drawn in his hand</hi> as <hi type="italic">captain of the host of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.5.13-Josh.5.14">Josh. v. 13, 14</reference>) and to John with his <hi type="italic">bow</hi> and his <hi type="italic">crown,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. Though the church was in a low condition, yet Christ was present in the midst of it. Was it hidden by the hills? He was much more hidden in the myrtle-grove, yet hidden as in an ambush, ready to appear for the seasonable relief of his people, to their happy surprise. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa. xlv. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">Israel's God and Saviour</hi> at the same time, their <hi type="italic">Holy One in the midst of them.</hi> He was <hi type="italic">riding,</hi> as a man of war, as a man in haste, <hi type="italic">riding on the heavens for the help</hi> of his people, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.26">Deut. xxxiii. 26</reference>. He rode on a <hi type="italic">red horse,</hi> either naturally so or dyed red with the blood of war, as this same victorious prince appeared <hi type="italic">red in his apparel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.2">Isa. lxiii. 1, 2</reference>. Red is a fiery colour, denoting that he is <hi type="italic">jealous for Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.14">v. 14</reference>) and very angry at her enemies. Christ, under the law, appeared on a red horse, denoting the terror of that dispensation, and that he had yet his conflict before him, when he was to <hi type="italic">resist unto blood.</hi> But, under the gospel, he appears on <hi type="italic">a white horse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">and again ch. xix. 11</reference>), denoting that he has now gained the victory, and rides in triumph, and hangs out the white, not the bloody flag. 3. He saw a troop of horse attending him, ready to receive and obey his orders: <hi type="italic">Behind him there were some red horses, and</hi> some <hi type="italic">speckled, and</hi> some <hi type="italic">white,</hi> angels attending the Lord Jesus, ready to be employed by him for the service of his church, some in acts of judgment, others of mercy, others in mixed events. Note, The King of the church has angels at command, not only to do him honour, but to minister for the good of those that are his. 4. He enquired into the signification of this vision. He had an angel talking with him, as his instructor, besides those he saw in the vision; so had Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">ch. xl. 3</reference>), and Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">ch. viii. 16</reference>. Zechariah asked him (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">O my Lord! what are these?</hi> And, it should seem this <hi type="italic">angel that talked with him</hi> was Christ himself, the <hi type="italic">man on the red horse,</hi> whom the rest were attendants on; to him immediately Zechariah addresses himself. Would we be acquainted with the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, we must make our application, not to angels (they are themselves learners), but to Christ himself, who is alone <hi type="italic">able to take the book, and open the seals,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.5.7">Rev. v. 7</reference>. The prophet's question implies a humble acknowledgment of his own ignorance and an earnest desire to be informed. O let me know what these are! This he desired, not for the satisfying of his curiosity, but that he might be furnished with something proper for the comfort and encouragement of the people of God, in their present distress. 5. He received from the <hi type="italic">angel that talked with</hi> him (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.9">v. 9</reference>), and from <hi type="italic">the man that stood among the myrtle-trees</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.10">v. 10</reference>), the interpretation of this vision. Note, Jesus Christ is ready to instruct those that are humbly desirous to be taught the things of God. He immediately said, <hi type="italic">I will show thee what these are.</hi> What knowledge we have, or may have, concerning the world of spirits, we are indebted to Christ for. The account given him was, <hi type="italic">These are those whom the Lord has sent:</hi> they are his messengers, his envoys, appointed (as his eyes are said to do, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>) to <hi type="italic">walk,</hi> to <hi type="italic">run,</hi> to fly swiftly <hi type="italic">through the earth,</hi> to observe what is done in it and to execute the divine commands. God needs them not, but he is pleased to employ them, and we need the comfort arising from the doctrine of their administration. <div eID="gen20769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20770" type="x-p"/> II. What the prophet heard, and what instructions were thereby given him. Faith comes by hearing, and, generally, in visions there was something said. <div eID="gen20770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20771" type="x-p"/> 1. He heard the report or representation which the angels made to Christ of the present state of the world, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.11">v. 11</reference>. They had been out abroad, as flying posts (<hi type="italic">being hastened by the King of kings' commandment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.3.15">Esth. iii. 15</reference>), and, having returned, they give this account to the <hi type="italic">Angel that stood among the myrtle-trees</hi> (for to the Lord Jesus angels themselves are accountable): <hi type="italic">We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold all the earth sits still and is at rest.</hi> We are taught to pray that the will of God may be done by men on earth as it is done by the angels in heaven; and here we see what need we have to pray so, for it is far from being so. For, (1.) We find the world of angels here very busy. Those that are employed in the court above rest not day nor night from praising God, which is their business there; and those that are employed in the camp below are never idle, nor lose time; they are still <hi type="italic">ascending and descending</hi> upon <hi type="italic">the Son of man</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.51">John i. 51</reference>, as on Jacob's ladder, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.12">Gen. xxviii. 12</reference>); they are still <hi type="italic">walking to and fro through the earth.</hi> Thus active, thus industrious, <hi type="italic">Satan</hi> owns himself to be in doing mischief, <reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>. It is well for us that good angels bestir themselves as much to do good, and that here in this earth we have guardians going about continually seeking to do us a kindness, as we have adversaries which, as roaring lions, go about continually, seeking to devour us. Though holy angels in this earth meet with a great deal that is disagreeable, yet, while they are going on God's errands, they hesitate not to <hi type="italic">walk to and fro through it.</hi> Their own habitation, which those that fell liked not, they will like the better when they return. (2.) We find the world of mankind here very careless: <hi type="italic">All the earth sits still, and is at rest,</hi> while all the church is made uneasy, <hi type="italic">tossed with tempests and not comforted.</hi> Those that are strangers to the church are secure; those that are enemies to it are successful. The Chaldeans and Persians dwell at ease, while the poor Jews are continually alarmed; as when <hi type="italic">the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city Shushan was perplexed.</hi> The children of men are merry and jovial, but <hi type="italic">none grieve for the affliction</hi> of God's children. Note, It is sad to think what a deep sleep the world is cast into, what a spirit of slumber has seized the generality of mankind, that are under God's wrath and Satan's power, and yet secure and unconcerned! They sit still and are at rest, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.26">Luke xvii. 26</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen20771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20772" type="x-p"/> 2. He heard Christ's intercession with the Father for his afflicted church, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">v. 12</reference>. The angels related the posture of affairs in this lower world, but we read not of any prayers they made for the redress of the grievances they had made a remonstrance of. No; it is <hi type="italic">the Angel among the myrtle-trees</hi> that is the great intercessor. Upon the report of the angels he immediately turned heavenward, and said, <hi type="italic">Lord, wilt thou not have mercy</hi> on thy church? (1.) The thing he intercedes for is <hi type="italic">mercy;</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">Ps. lxxxv. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Show us thy mercy, O Lord!</hi> Note, God's mercy is all in all to the church's comfort; and all his mercy must be hoped for through Christ's mediation. (2.) The thing he complains of is the delay of this mercy: <hi type="italic">How long wilt thou not have mercy!</hi> He knows that <hi type="italic">mercies</hi> through him <hi type="italic">shall be built up for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.2">Ps. lxxxix. 2</reference>), but thinks it long that the building is deferred. (3.) The objects of compassion recommended to the divine mercies are, Jerusalem, the holy city, and the other cities of Judah that were now in ruins; for God had had <hi type="italic">indignation against them</hi> now <hi type="italic">threescore and ten years.</hi> He mentions seventy years because that was the time fixed in the divine councils for the continuance of the captivity; so long the indignation lasted, and though <hi type="italic">now for a little space grace</hi> had been <hi type="italic">shown them from the Lord their God,</hi> to <hi type="italic">give them some reviving</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>), yet the scars of those seventy years' captivity still remained so deep, so painful, that this is the melancholy string they still harp upon—the divine indignation during those seventy years. Dr. Lightfoot thinks that whereas the seventy years of the captivity were reckoned from Jehoiakim's fourth year, and ended in the first of Cyrus, these seventy years are to be computed from the eleventh of Zedekiah, when Jerusalem and the temple were burnt, about nineteen years after the first captivity, and which ended in this second year of Darius Hystaspes, about seventeen years after Cyrus's proclamation, as that seventy years mentioned <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">ch. vii. 5</reference> was about nineteen years after; the captivity went off, as it came on, gradually. "Lord, we are still under the burden of the seventy years' wrath, <hi type="italic">and wilt thou be angry with us for ever?</hi>" <div eID="gen20772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20773" type="x-p"/> 3. He heard a gracious reply given to this intercession of Christ's for his church; for it is a prevailing intercession, always acceptable, <hi type="italic">and him the Father heareth always</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord answered the angel,</hi> this angel of the covenant, <hi type="italic">with good words and comfortable words,</hi> with promises of mercy and deliverance, and the perfecting of what he had begun in favour to them. These were comfortable words to Christ, who is grieved in the grievances of his church, and comfortable to all that mourn with Zion. God often answers prayer with good words, when he does not immediately appear in great works; and those good words are real answers to prayer. Men's good words will not feed the body (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 16</reference>), but God's good words will feed the faith, for saying and doing with him are not two things, though they are with us. <div eID="gen20773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20774" type="x-p"/> 4. He heard that reply which was given to the angel repeated to himself, with a commission to publish it to the children of his people, for their comfort. <hi type="italic">The revelation of Jesus Christ which God gave to him</hi> he <hi type="italic">signified to his servant John,</hi> and by him <hi type="italic">to the churches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">4</reference>. Thus all the good words and comfortable words of the gospel we receive from Jesus Christ, as he received them from the Father, in answer to the prayer of his blood, and his ministers are appointed to preach them <hi type="italic">to all the world.</hi> Now that God would <hi type="italic">speak comfortably to Jerusalem,</hi> Zechariah is <hi type="italic">the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare you the way of the Lord. The voice said, Cry. Cry then.</hi> The prophets must now cry as loudly to show God's people their comforts as ever they did formerly to show them <hi type="italic">their transgressions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2-Isa.40.3">Isa. xl. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">6</reference>. And if he ask, <hi type="italic">What shall I cry?</hi> he is here instructed. (1.) He must proclaim the wrath God has in store for the enemies of Jerusalem. He is <hi type="italic">jealous for Zion with great jealousy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.1.14">v. 14</reference>. He takes himself to be highly affronted by the injuries and indignities that are done to his church, as he had been formerly by the iniquities found in his church. The earth <hi type="italic">sat still and was at rest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.11">v. 11</reference>), not relenting at all, nor showing the least remorse, for all the mischief they had done to Jerusalem, as Joseph's brethren, who, when they had sold him, sat down to eat bread; and this God took very ill (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am very sorely displeased with the heathen, that are at ease,</hi> and have no concern for the afflicted church. Much more will he be displeased with those that are <hi type="italic">at ease in Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amos vi. 1</reference>), with Zion's own sons, that sympathize not with her in her sorrows. But this was not all; they were not only not concerned for her, but they were concerned against her: <hi type="italic">I was but a little displeased</hi> with my people, and designed to correct them moderately, but those that were employed as instruments of the correction cast off all pity, and with the greatest rage and malice <hi type="italic">helped forward the affliction</hi> and added to it, <hi type="italic">persecuting those whom God had smitten</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>) and insulting over those whom he had troubled. See <reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Isa. xlvii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">x. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12-Ezek.25.15">Ezek. xxv. 12, 15</reference>. Note, God is displeased with those who help forward the affliction even of such as suffer justly; for true humanity, in such a case, is good divinity. (2.) He must proclaim the mercy God has in store for Jerusalem and the <hi type="italic">cities of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.1.16">v. 16</reference>. He must cry, "<hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord, I have returned to Jerusalem with mercies.</hi> I was going away in wrath, but I am now returning in love. <hi type="italic">Cry yet</hi> to the same purport," <reference osisRef="Zech.1.17">v. 17</reference>. There must now be line upon line for consolation, as formerly there had been for conviction. <hi type="italic">The Lord,</hi> even the Lord of hosts, assures them, [1.] That the temple shall be built that is now but in the building. This good work which they are now about, though it meet with much discouragement, shall be perfected, and they shall have the tokens of God's presence, and opportunities of conversing with him, and worshipping him, as formerly. Note, It is good news indeed to any place to hear that God will build his house in it. [2.] That Jerusalem shall again be <hi type="italic">built as a city compact together,</hi> which had formerly been its glory, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.3">Ps. cxxii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">A line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem,</hi> in order to the rebuilding of it with great exactness and uniformity. [3.] That the nation shall again become populous and rich, though now diminished and impoverished. Not only Jerusalem, but other cities that are reduced and lie in a little compass, shall yet <hi type="italic">spread abroad,</hi> or be diffused; their suburbs shall extend far, and colonies shall be transplanted from them; and this <hi type="italic">through prosperity:</hi> they shall be so numerous, and so wealthy, that there shall not be room for them; they shall complain that <hi type="italic">the place is too strait,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.20">Isa. xlix. 20</reference>. As they had been scattered and spread abroad, through their calamities, so they should now be through their prosperity. <hi type="italic">Let thy fountains be dispersed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.16">Prov. v. 16</reference>. The cities that should thus increase God calls his cities; they are <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> by him, and they are <hi type="italic">fruitful and multiply, and replenish the land.</hi> [4.] That all their present sorrows should not only be balanced, but for ever silenced, by divine consolations: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall yet comfort Zion.</hi> Yet at length, though her griefs and grievances may continue long, God has comforts in reserve for Zion and all her mourners. [5.] That all this will be the fruit of God's preventing distinguishing favour: He shall yet <hi type="italic">choose Jerusalem,</hi> shall renew his choice, renew his covenant, shall make it appear that he has chosen Jerusalem. As he first built them up into a people when he brought them out of Egypt, so he will now rebuild them, when he brings them out of Babylon, not for any worthiness of theirs, but in pursuance of his own choice, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 7, 8</reference>. Jerusalem is the city he has chosen, and he will not cast it off.
entries.e8eb0e571fdd2c4c47fdae74c254db8d26da33df: <div eID="gen20774" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Comfort for Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20775" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then lifted I up mine eyes, and saw, and behold four horns. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I said unto the angel that talked with me, What <hi type="italic">be</hi> these? And he answered me, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the horns which have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shewed me four carpenters. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then said I, What come these to do? And he spake, saying, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the horns which have scattered Judah, so that no man did lift up his head: but these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up <hi type="italic">their</hi> horn over the land of Judah to scatter it. <div eID="gen20775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20776" type="x-p"/> It is the comfort and triumph of the church (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.19">Isa. lix. 19</reference>) that <hi type="italic">when the enemy shall come in like a flood,</hi> with mighty force and fury, then the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord shall lift up a standard against him.</hi> Now, in this vision (the second which this prophet had), we have an illustration of that, God's Spirit making a stand, and making head, against the formidable power of the church's adversaries. <div eID="gen20776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20777" type="x-p"/> I. We have here the enemies of the church bold and daring, and threatening to be its death, to <hi type="italic">cut off the name of Israel;</hi> such the people of God had lately been insulted by: <hi type="italic">I looked and behold four horns</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.18">v. 18</reference>), which are explained <reference osisRef="Zech.1.19">v. 19</reference>. They <hi type="italic">are the horns which have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem,</hi> that is, the Jews both in the country and in the city, because they were the Israel of God. They have <hi type="italic">tossed them</hi> (so some read it), as furious bulls with their horns toss that which they are enraged at. They have scattered them, <hi type="italic">so that no man did lift up his head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.1.21">v. 21</reference>. No man durst show his face for fear of them, much less give them any opposition, or make head against them. They are <hi type="italic">horns,</hi> denoting their dignity and dominion—<hi type="italic">horns exalted,</hi> denoting also their strength, and power, and violence. They are <hi type="italic">four horns,</hi> for the Jews are surrounded with them on every side; when they avoid one horn that pushes at them they run upon another. The men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and many of Israel that joined themselves to them, set about the building of the temple; but the enemies of that work from all sides pushed at them, and drove them from it. Rehum, and Shimshai, and the other Samaritans that opposed the building of the temple, were these horns, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.8">Ezra iv. 8</reference>. So were Sanballat and Tobiah, and the Ammonites and Arabians, that opposed the building of the wall, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.7">Neh. iv. 7</reference>. Note, The church's enemies have horns, and use them to the hindrance of every good work. The great enemy of the New-Testament church has <hi type="italic">seven heads and ten horns</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Rev. xvii. 3</reference>), so that those who endeavour to do the church any service must expect to be pushed at. <div eID="gen20777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20778" type="x-p"/> II. We have here the friends of the church active and prevailing. The prophet did himself lift up his eyes and see the four horns, and saw them so formidable that he began to despair of the safety of every good man, and the success of every good work; but <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> then <hi type="italic">showed him four carpenters,</hi> or <hi type="italic">smiths,</hi> who were empowered to cut off these horns, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.20-Zech.1.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. With an eye of sense we see the power of the enemies of the church; look which way we will, the world shows us that. But it is with an eye of faith that we see it safe, notwithstanding; it is the Lord that shows us that, as he opened the eyes of the prophet's servant to see the angelic guards round about his master, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings vi. 17</reference>. Observe, Those that were to fray or break the horns of the Gentiles, and to cast them out, were, 1. <hi type="italic">Carpenters</hi> or <hi type="italic">smiths</hi> (for they are supposed by some to have been horns of iron), men who had skill and ability to do it, whose proper business it was, and who understood their business and had tools at hand to do it with. Note, God calls those to serve the interests of his church whom he either finds, or makes, fit for it. If there be horns (which denote the force and fury of beasts) against the church, there are carpenters (which denote the wisdom and forecast of men) for the church, by which they find ways to master the strongest beasts, for <hi type="italic">every kind of beasts is tamed, and has been tamed, of mankind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.7">Jam. iii. 7</reference>. 2. They were <hi type="italic">four carpenters,</hi> as many horns so many hands to saw them off. Note, Which way soever the church is threatened with mischief, and opposition given to its interests, God can find out ways and means to check the force, to restrain the wrath, and make it turn to his praise. Some by these four carpenters understand Zerubbabel and Joshua, Ezra and Nehemiah, who carried on the work of God in spite of the opposition given to it. Those horned beasts broke into God's vineyard to tread it down; but the good magistrates and the good ministers whom God raised up, though they had not power to <hi type="italic">cut off the horns of the wicked</hi> (as David did, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Ps. lxxv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">10</reference>), yet frightened them and cast them out. Note, When God has work to do he will raise up some to do it and others to defend it and protect those that are employed in the doing of it.  <chapter eID="Zech.1"/> <div eID="gen20778" type="x-p"/>

entries.5ee0b084357f221e4927f97e386a4debff79c921: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13010"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> The name Zechariah means one whom Jehovah remembers: a common name, four others of the same name occurring in the Old Testament. Like Jeremiah and Ezekiel, he was a priest as well as a prophet, which adapts him for the sacerdotal character of some of his prophecies (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>). He is called "the son of Berechiah the son of Iddo" (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zec 1:1</reference>); but simply "the son of Iddo" in <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1">Ezr 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.14">6:14</reference>. Probably his father died when he was young; and hence, as sometimes occurs in Jewish genealogies, he is called "the son of Iddo," his grandfather. Iddo was one of the priests who returned to Zerubbabel and Joshua from Babylon (<reference osisRef="Neh.12.4">Ne 12:4</reference>).<div eID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24402" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zechariah entered early on his prophetic functions (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.4">Zec 2:4</reference>); only two months later than Haggai, in the second year of Darius' reign, 520 B.C. The design of both prophets was to encourage the people and their religious and civil leaders, Joshua and Zerubbabel, in their work of rebuilding the temple, after the interruption caused by the Samaritans (see Introduction to Haggai). Zechariah does so especially by unfolding in detail the glorious future in connection with the present depressed appearance of the theocracy, and its visible symbol, the temple. He must have been very young in leaving Babylonia, where he was born. The Zechariah, son of Barachias, mentioned by our Lord (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Mt 23:35</reference>) as slain between the porch and the altar, must have been the one called the son of Jehoiada in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.21">2Ch 24:21</reference>, who so perished: the same person often had two names; and our Lord, in referring to the Hebrew Bible, of which Second Chronicles is the last book, would naturally mention the last martyr in the Hebrew order of the canon, as He had instanced Abel as the first. Owing to <reference osisRef="Matt.27.9">Mt 27:9</reference> quoting <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference> as the words of Jeremiah, Mede doubts the authenticity of the ninth through the fourteenth chapters, and ascribes them to Jeremiah: he thinks that these chapters were not found till after the return from the captivity, and being approved by Zechariah, were added to his prophecies, as Agur's Proverbs were added to those of Solomon. All the oldest authorities, except two manuscripts of the old Italian or Pre-Vulgate version, read Jeremiah in <reference osisRef="Matt.27.9">Mt 27:9</reference>. The quotation there is not to the letter copied from Zechariah, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.1">Jr 18:1</reference>, 2; 32:6-12, may also have been in the mind of Matthew, and perhaps in the mind of Zechariah, whence the former mentions Jeremiah. Hengstenberg similarly thinks that Matthew names Jeremiah, rather than Zechariah, to turn attention to the fact that Zechariah's prophecy is but a reiteration of the fearful oracle in <reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.19.15">Jr 18:1-19:15</reference>, to be fulfilled in the destruction of the Jewish nation. Jeremiah had already, by the image of a potter's vessel, portrayed their ruin in Nebuchadnezzar's invasion; and as Zechariah virtually repeats this threat, to be inflicted again under Messiah for the nation's rejection of Him, Matthew, virtually, by mentioning Jeremiah, implies that the "field of blood" [Mt 27:8, 9], now bought by "the reward of iniquity" [Ac 1:18] in the valley of Hinnom, was long ago a scene of prophetic doom in which awful disaster had been symbolically predicted: that the present purchase of that field with the traitor's price renewed the prophecy and revived the curse--</hi>a curse pronounced of old by Jeremiah, and once fulfilled in the Babylonian siege--a curse reiterated by Zechariah, and again to be verified in the Roman desolation. Lightfoot (referring to B. Bathra and Kimchi) less probably thinks the third division of Scripture, the prophets, began with Jeremiah, and that the whole body of prophets is thus quoted by the name "Jeremiah." The mention of "Ephraim" and "Israel" in these chapters as distinct from Judah, does not prove that the prophecy was written while the ten tribes existed as a separate kingdom. It rather implies that hereafter not only Judah, but the ten tribes also, shall be restored, the earnest of which was given in the numbers out of the ten tribes who returned with their brethren the Jews from captivity under Cyrus. There is nothing in these characters to imply that a king reigned in Judah at that time. The editor of the Hebrew canon joined these chapters to Zechariah, not to Jeremiah; the Septuagint, three hundred years B.C., confirms this.<div eID="gen24404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24405" type="x-p"/> The prophecy consists of four parts: (1) Introductory, Zec 1:1-6. (2) Symbolical, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.7">Zec 1:7</reference>, to the end of the sixth chapter, containing nine visions; all these were vouchsafed in one night, and are of a symbolical character. (3) Didactic, the seventh and eighth chapters containing an answer to a query of the Beth-elites concerning a certain feast. And (4) Prophetic, the ninth chapter to the end. These six last chapters predict Alexander's expedition along the west coast of Palestine to Egypt; God's protection of the Jews, both at that time and under the Maccabees; the advent, sufferings, and reign of Messiah; the destruction of Jerusalem by Rome, and dissolution of the Jews' polity; their conversion and restoration; the overthrow of the wicked confederacy which assailed them in Canaan; and the Gentiles' joining in their holy worship [Henderson]. The difference in style between the former and the latter chapters is due to the difference of subject; the first six chapters being of a symbolical and peculiar character, while the poetical style of the concluding chapters is adapted admirably to the subjects treated. The titles (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.1">Zec 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.1">12:1</reference>) accord with the prophetic matter which follows; nor is it necessary for unity of authorship that the introductory formulas occurring in the first eight chapters should occur in the last six. The non-reference in the last six chapters to the completion of the temple and the Jews' restoration after the captivity is just what we should expect, if, as seems likely, these chapters were written long after the completion of the temple and the restoration of the Jews' polity after the captivity, in circumstances different from those which engaged the prophet when he wrote the earlier chapters.<div eID="gen24405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The style varies with the subject: at one time conversational, at another poetical. His symbols are enigmatical and are therefore accompanied with explanations. His prose is like that of Ezekiel--</hi>diffuse, uniform, and repetitious. The rhythm is somewhat unequal, and the parallelisms are not altogether symmetrical. Still, there is found often much of the elevation met with in the earlier prophets, and a general congruity between the style and the subjects. Graphic vividness is his peculiar merit. Chaldæisms occur occasionally. Another special characteristic of Zechariah is his introduction of spiritual beings into his prophetic scenes.<div eID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.1.1-Zech.1.17">Zec 1:1-17</reference>. Introductory Exhortation to Repentance. The Visions. The man among the myrtles: Comforting explanation by the angel, an encouragement to the Jews to build the city and temple: The four horns and four artificers.</title> <div sID="gen24407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13010"/>1. See Introduction. <div eID="gen24407" type="x-p"/>
entries.792305f8076a7277afa256ab40317c5822374fcc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13011"/><div sID="gen24408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13011"/>2. God fulfilled His threats against your fathers; beware, then, lest by disregarding His voice by me, as they did in the case of former prophets, ye suffer like them. The special object Zechariah aims at is that they should awake from their selfish negligence to obey God's command to rebuild His temple (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.4-Hag.1.8">Hag 1:4-8</reference>).<div eID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sore displeased--</hi>Hebrew, "displeased with a displeasure," that is, vehemently, with no common displeasure, exhibited in the destruction of the Jews' city and in their captivity. <div eID="gen24409" type="x-p"/>
entries.63c08caedd71244749455c85c3374197a3acb148: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13012"/><div sID="gen24410" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13012"/><hi type="bold">3. saith the Lord of hosts--</hi>a phrase frequent in Haggai and Zechariah, implying God's boundless resources and universal power, so as to inspire the Jews with confidence to work.<div eID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Turn ye unto me ... and I will turn--</hi>that is, and then, as the sure consequence, "I will turn unto you" (Mal 3:7; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">Jas 4:8</reference>; compare also <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jr 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.30">Eze 18:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">Mi 7:19</reference>). Though God hath brought you back from captivity, yet this state will not last long unless ye are really converted. God has heavier scourges ready, and has begun to give symptoms of displeasure [Calvin]. (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24411" type="x-p"/>
entries.a44732e60cbb30618aaca2ecab358fc272abec3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13013"/><div sID="gen24412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13013"/><hi type="bold">4. Be ye not as your fathers--</hi>The Jews boasted of their fathers; but he shows that their fathers were refractory, and that ancient example and long usage will not justify disobedience (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.15">2Ch 36:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the former prophets--</hi>those who lived before the captivity. It aggravated their guilt that, not only had they the law, but they had been often called to repent by God's prophets. <div eID="gen24413" type="x-p"/>
entries.99534f0ca781f59065240c8079794f9ff2551945: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13014"/><div sID="gen24414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13014"/><hi type="bold">5. Your fathers ... and the prophets, do they live for ever?--</hi>In contrast to "My words" (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.6">Zec 1:6</reference>), which "endure for ever" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.25">1Pe 1:25</reference>). "Your fathers have perished, as was foretold; and their fate ought to warn you. But you may say, The prophets too are dead. I grant it, but still My words do not die: though dead, their prophetical words from Me, fulfilled against your fathers, are not dead with them. Beware, then, lest ye share their fate." <div eID="gen24414" type="x-p"/>
entries.c65f73dc9e89878fbf14c7667d11720eb3421337: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13015"/><div sID="gen24415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13015"/><hi type="bold">6. statutes--</hi>My determined purposes to punish for sin.<div eID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which I commanded my servants--</hi>namely, to announce to your fathers.<div eID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did they not take hold--</hi>that is, overtake, as a foe overtakes one fleeing.<div eID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they returned--</hi>Turning from their former self-satisfaction, they recognized their punishment as that which God's prophets had foretold.<div eID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thought to do--</hi>that is, decreed to do. Compare with this verse <reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">La 2:17</reference>.<div eID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our ways--</hi>evil ways (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.18">Jr 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">23:2</reference>). <div eID="gen24420" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8654347c8f214425add528571e7be4c259d7e17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13016"/><div sID="gen24421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13016"/>7. The general plan of the nine following visions (Zec 1:8-6:15) is first to present the symbol; then, on a question being put, to subjoin the interpretation. Though the visions are distinct, they form one grand whole, presented in one night to the prophet's mind, two or three months after the prophet's first commission (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zec 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sebat--</hi>the eleventh month of the Jewish year, from the new moon in February to the new moon in March. The term is Chaldee, meaning a "shoot," namely, the month when trees begin to shoot or bud. <div eID="gen24422" type="x-p"/>
entries.be01203fe3b9a255403e2004ceec4cd45a865b69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13017"/><div sID="gen24423" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13017"/><hi type="bold">8. by night--</hi>The Jews begin their day with sunset; therefore the night which preceded the twenty-fourth day of the month is meant (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.7">Zec 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man--</hi>Jehovah, the second person of the Trinity, manifested in man's form, an earnest of the incarnation; called the "angel of Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.11">Zec 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), "Jehovah the angel of the covenant" (Mal 3:1; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.16.7">Ge 16:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zec 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.22.11">Ge 22:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.3.2">Ex 3:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Zech.1.4">Zec 1:4</reference>). Being at once divine and human, He must be God and man in one person.<div eID="gen24424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">riding--</hi>implying swiftness in executing God's will in His providence; hastening to help His people.<div eID="gen24425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">red horse--</hi>the color that represents bloodshed: implying vengeance to be inflicted on the foes of Israel (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.22">2Ki 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.4">Re 6:4</reference>); also fiery zeal.<div eID="gen24426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the myrtle trees--</hi>symbol of the Jewish Church: not a stately cedar, but a lowly, though fragrant, myrtle. It was its depressed state that caused the Jews to despond; this vision is designed to cheer them with better hopes. The uncreated angel of Jehovah's presence standing (as His abiding place, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Psa 132:14</reference>) among them, is a guarantee for her safety, lowly though she now be.<div eID="gen24427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the bottom--</hi>in a low place or bottom of a river; alluding to Babylon near the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, the scene of Judah's captivity. The myrtle delights in low places and the banks of waters [Pembellus]. Maurer translates, from a different root, "in a shady place."<div eID="gen24428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24429" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">red horses--</hi>that is, horsemen mounted on red horses; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.10">Zec 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>, confirm this view.<div eID="gen24429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speckled ... white--</hi>The "white" implies triumph and victory for Judah; "speckled" (from a root "to intertwine"), a combination of the two colors white and red (bay [Moore]), implies a state of things mixed, partly prosperous, partly otherwise [Henderson]; or, the connection of the wrath (answering to the "red") about to fall on the Jews' foes, and triumph (answering to the "white") to the Jews themselves in God's arrangements for His people [Moore]. Some angels ("the red horses") exercised offices of vengeance; others ("the white"), those of joy; others ("the speckled"), those of a mixed character (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.6.2">Zec 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.3">3</reference>). God has ministers of every kind for promoting the interests of His Church. <div eID="gen24430" type="x-p"/>
entries.780d89a831e85ab3e55a1b9f583cad49c29f71b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13018"/><div sID="gen24431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13018"/><hi type="bold">9. the angel that talked with me--</hi>not the "man upon the red horse," as is evident from <reference osisRef="Zech.1.10">Zec 1:10</reference>, where he (the Divine Angel) is distinguished from the "angel that talked with me" (the phrase used of him, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zec 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.3">Zec 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.4">6:4</reference>), that is, the interpreting angel. The Hebrew for "with me," or, "in me" (<reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Nu 12:8</reference>), implies internal, intimate communication [Jerome].<div eID="gen24431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">show thee--</hi>reveal to thy mental vision. <div eID="gen24432" type="x-p"/>
entries.d534d5bca8b98ba71d174a0138198759df455541: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13019"/><div sID="gen24433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13019"/><hi type="bold">10. answered--</hi>The "angel of the covenant" here gives the reply instead of the interpreting angel, to imply that all communications through the interpreting angel come from Him as their source.<div eID="gen24433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth--</hi>If "Satan walks to and fro in the earth" (implying restless activity) on errands of mischief to God's people (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>), the Lord sends other angels to "walk to and fro" with unceasing activity everywhere to counterwork Satan's designs, and to defend His people (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.11">91:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">103:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">He 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen24434" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe1b78f627b2d5454d5a02465379ca324774acbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13020"/><div sID="gen24435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13020"/>11. The attendant angels report to the Lord of angels, "the earth ... is at rest." The flourishing state of the heathen "earth," while Judah was desolate and its temple not yet restored, is the powerful plea in the Divine Angel's intercession with God the Father in <reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>. When Judah was depressed to the lowest point, and the heathen elated to the highest, it was time for Jehovah to work for His people.<div eID="gen24435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sitteth still--</hi>dwells surely. <div eID="gen24436" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1e6ee213ce99257c10ddfa245aa1ebbdaee3838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13021"/><div sID="gen24437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13021"/>12. Not only does Messiah stand among His people (the "myrtles," <reference osisRef="Zech.1.8">Zec 1:8</reference>), but intercedes for them with the Father ("Lord," or "Jehovah of hosts") effectively (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zec 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">He 7:25</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.20">Psa 102:13-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>, as to Judah's restoration in answer to prayer.<div eID="gen24437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answered and said--</hi>said in continuation of the discourse: proceeded to say.<div eID="gen24438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how long--</hi>Messiah's people pray similarly to their Head. <reference osisRef="Rev.6.10">Re 6:10</reference>, "How long," &c. Heretofore it was vain to pray, but now that the divinely appointed "threescore and ten years" (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>) are elapsed, it is time to pray to Thee for the fulfilment of Thy promise, seeing that Thy grace is not yet fully manifested, nor Thy promise fulfilled. God's promises are not to make us slothful, but to quicken our prayers. Henderson, dating the seventy years from the destruction of Jerusalem (588 B.C.), supposes two years of the seventy had yet to run (520 B.C.). <div eID="gen24439" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb4b7d7f5e159af7082f4d8cb0048a6abf236130: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13022"/><div sID="gen24440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13022"/><hi type="bold">13. the Lord--</hi>Jehovah, called "the angel of the Lord (Jehovah)" (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen24440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good words and comfortable words--</hi>literally, "words, consolations." The subject of these consolatory words is stated in <reference osisRef="Zech.1.14">Zec 1:14</reference>, &c.; the promise of full re-establishment, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jr 29:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">11</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.57.18">Is 57:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8">Ho 11:8</reference>). <div eID="gen24441" type="x-p"/>
entries.63d32ac7f91e63f5b0159a21568e258c0ccaf963: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13023"/><div sID="gen24442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13023"/><hi type="bold">14. Cry--</hi>Proclaim so as to be heard clearly by all (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Is 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">58:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am jealous for Jerusalem--</hi>As a husband jealous for his wife, wronged by others, so Jehovah is for Judah, who has been injured wantonly by the heathen (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.2">Zec 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.25.11">Nu 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.25.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.10">1Ki 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.18">Joe 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen24443" type="x-p"/>
entries.b70c6550fee2c82031b27791251a78718b148d16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13024"/><div sID="gen24444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13024"/><hi type="bold">15. very sore displeased with the heathen--</hi>in contrast with "I was but a little displeased" with My people. God's displeasure with His people is temporary and for their chastening; with the heathen oppressors, it is final and fatal (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jr 30:11</reference>). God's instruments for chastising His people, when He has done with them, He casts into the fire.<div eID="gen24444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are at ease--</hi>carnally secure. A stronger phrase than "is at rest" (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.11">Zec 1:11</reference>). They are "at ease," but as I am "sore displeased" with them, their ease is accursed. Judah is in "affliction," but as I love her and am jealous for her, she has every reason to be encouraged in prosecuting the temple work.<div eID="gen24445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">helped forward the affliction--</hi>afflicted My people more than I desired. The heathen sought the utter extinction of Judah to gratify their own ambition and revenge (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Is 47:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.3">Eze 25:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.6">6</reference>; Ob 10-17). <div eID="gen24446" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e33b36c3a5eb8bcebd4c2d590f7d7e55b574fd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13025"/><div sID="gen24447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13025"/><hi type="bold">16. I am returned--</hi>whereas in anger I had before withdrawn from her (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen24447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with mercies--</hi>not merely of one kind, nor once only, but repeated mercies.<div eID="gen24448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my house shall be built--</hi>which at this time (the second year of Darius, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zec 1:1</reference>) had only its foundations laid (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.18">Hag 2:18</reference>). It was not completed till the sixth year of Darius (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.15">Ezr 6:15</reference>).<div eID="gen24449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">line--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.38.5">Job 38:5</reference>). The measuring-line for building, not hastily, but with measured regularity. Not only the temple, but Jerusalem also was to be rebuilt (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.3">Ne 2:3</reference>, &c.; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.2.1">Zec 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>). Also, as to the future temple and city, <reference osisRef="Ezek.41.3">Eze 41:3</reference>; 42:1-44:31; 45:6. <div eID="gen24450" type="x-p"/>
entries.cad561300fed878713deb3ce27da9345e7fb80c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13026"/><div sID="gen24451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13026"/><hi type="bold">17. yet--</hi>though heretofore lying in abject prostration.<div eID="gen24451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">My cities--</hi>not only Jerusalem, but the subordinate cities of Judah. God claims them all as peculiarly His, and therefore will restore them.<div eID="gen24452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through prosperity ... spread abroad--</hi>or overflow; metaphor from an overflowing vessel or fountain (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.5.16">Pr 5:16</reference>) [Pembellus]. Abundance of fruits of the earth, corn and wine, and a large increase of citizens, are meant; also spiritual prosperity.<div eID="gen24453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comfort Zion--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Is 40:1</reference>, 2; 51:3).<div eID="gen24454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choose--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.2.12">Zec 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">Is 14:1</reference>). Here meaning, "show by acts of loving-kindness that He has chosen." His immutable choice from everlasting is the fountain whence flow all such particular acts of love. <div eID="gen24455" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f3c5ab1bcae9876cde7ec8695c12bf44bfbf313: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13027"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.1.18-Zech.1.21">Zec 1:18-21</reference>. Second Vision. The power of the Jews foes shall be dissipated.</title> <div sID="gen24456" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13027"/><hi type="bold">18. four horns--</hi>To a pastoral people like the Jews the horns of the strongest in the herd naturally suggested a symbol of power and pride of conscious strength: hence the ruling powers of the world (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.12">12</reference>). The number four in Zechariah's time referred to the four cardinal points of the horizon. Wherever God's people turned, there were foes to encounter (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.7">Ne 4:7</reference>); the Assyrian, Chaldean, and Samaritan on the north; Egypt and Arabia on the south; Philistia on the west; Ammon and Moab on the east.
